entries.source: Conway’s Game of Life is played on a grid of square cells. Each cell is either alive or empty. To find the next generation, count each cell’s neighbours: the eight cells that touch it, diagonals included. Then apply four rules.
entries.context: P content. Preserve any inline HTML tags and attributes.

entries.source: Loneliness. A living cell with fewer than two living neighbours dies.
entries.context: LI content. Preserve any inline HTML tags and attributes.

entries.source: Survival. A living cell with two or three living neighbours stays alive.
entries.context: LI content. Preserve any inline HTML tags and attributes.

entries.source: Crowding. A living cell with more than three living neighbours dies.
entries.context: LI content. Preserve any inline HTML tags and attributes.

entries.source: Birth. An empty cell with exactly three living neighbours becomes alive.
entries.context: LI content. Preserve any inline HTML tags and attributes.

entries.source: Every cell is judged at the same moment, using only the current generation. The whole grid then changes at once. The mathematician John Conway devised the rules in 1970.
entries.context: P content. Preserve any inline HTML tags and attributes.

entries.source: The field here is finite: the left and right edges join, as do the top and bottom, so a pattern that leaves one side returns from the other. It starts from the R-pentomino, five cells that take 1,103 generations to settle on an unbounded grid. On a small, wrapped field they unfold differently, so use Step to follow the first few generations.
